root_cause.text: In the NetLabel unlabeled Generic Netlink parser, `netlbl_unlabel_addrinfo_get()` validated address size based only on the address attribute while relying on `NLA_BINARY` policies that enforce only maximum, not exact, lengths, so a shorter IPv4/IPv6 mask attribute could be accepted and later read as a full `struct in_addr`/`struct in6_addr`.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE/commit states the function “did not independently validate the corresponding mask attribute length” and that “NLA_BINARY policy lengths are maximum lengths by default”; the patch changes `NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4/6ADDR` and `NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4/6MASK` to `NLA_POLICY_EXACT_LEN(...)` and removes the old `nla_len()`-based checks in `netlbl_unlabel_addrinfo_get()`, showing the bug was insufficient exact-length validation of the mask attribute.

intent_record.intent_summary: Enforce exact netlink attribute lengths for IPv4/IPv6 address and mask fields to reject malformed NetLabel unlabeled messages.
intent_record.what: The NetLabel unlabeled generic netlink attribute policy entries for NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV6ADDR, NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV6MASK, NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4ADDR, and NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4MASK were changed from explicit NLA_BINARY definitions with a .len field to NLA_POLICY_EXACT_LEN(sizeof(struct in6_addr)) and NLA_POLICY_EXACT_LEN(sizeof(struct in_addr)) macros.
intent_record.how: This makes netlink validation require those IPv4 and IPv6 address and mask attributes to be exactly the expected structure size, rejecting messages with shorter or longer payloads instead of accepting any payload up to the specified length.

intent_record.intent_summary: Stop rejecting unlabel address netlink entries based on attribute payload lengths and use the fixed IPv4/IPv6 structure sizes directly.
intent_record.what: The function netlbl_unlabel_addrinfo_get() removes the local variable addr_len and deletes the nla_len() size checks for IPv4 and IPv6 address/mask attributes, replacing them with direct assignments of *len to sizeof(struct in_addr) for IPv4 and sizeof(struct in6_addr) for IPv6 before returning the attribute data pointers.
intent_record.how: At runtime, the function no longer validates netlink attribute payload lengths for the IPv4/IPv6 address and mask fields and instead always reports the expected fixed address size, allowing processing to continue without returning -EINVAL for mismatched attribute lengths.

Stop rejecting unlabel address netlink entries based on attribute payload lengths and use the fixed IPv4/IPv6 structure sizes directly.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly fixes the root cause by requiring exact IPv4/IPv6 netlink attribute lengths for both address and mask fields, preventing undersized mask attributes from being accepted and later over-read.

The change directly touches the same root cause area: address/mask length handling in the NetLabel unlabeled parser. It removes payload-length-based validation/rejection and instead uses fixed IPv4/IPv6 structure sizes, which is directly related to the bug caused by relying on insufficient netlink attribute length validation for address and mask attributes.

candidates.rationale: This validation is wrong because it only rejects when the IPv4 address length is both not the expected size and different from the mask length. As a result, a too-short mask matching a too-short address can pass, enabling later full-size reads.

This second half of the IPv4 check ties validity to equality with the mask length instead of requiring the mask to be exactly sizeof(struct in_addr), directly allowing undersized mask attributes when lengths match.
This IPv6 validation has the same flawed logic: it does not enforce exact size for both address and mask, so an undersized IPv6 mask can be accepted if it matches the address length.
This clause compares the IPv6 mask length only to addr_len rather than requiring sizeof(struct in6_addr), which is the direct reason malformed short mask attributes are accepted.

vuln_statements.explanation: This is the start of the flawed IPv4 length validation. By using a conjunction with the mask-length comparison instead of enforcing exact fixed size, it allows undersized IPv4 attributes to pass when the mask length matches the short address length.

This completes the IPv4 condition that validates the mask only by equality with addr_len, not by requiring sizeof(struct in_addr). That directly permits a too-short IPv4 mask to be accepted and later read as a full struct.

This is the analogous flawed IPv6 validation. It does not require exact IPv6 attribute size, only rejecting when the address is both wrong-sized and different from the mask length, so matching undersized inputs can pass.

This clause finishes the vulnerable IPv6 check by comparing mask length only to addr_len rather than sizeof(struct in6_addr), enabling undersized IPv6 mask attributes to be accepted before full-size reads.

bic_trace_step.reason: The relevant logic is fully visible in `netlbl_unlabel_addrinfo_get()`, so the snippet is sufficient. The vulnerability root cause is present because the function validates the length using only the address attribute and only checks that the mask length matches the address length when the address length is not the expected size. Specifically, for IPv4 it does `addr_len = nla_len(info->attrs[NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4ADDR]);` and then `if (addr_len != sizeof(struct in_addr) && addr_len != nla_len(info->attrs[NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV4MASK])) return -EINVAL;`. For IPv6 it similarly does `addr_len = nla_len(info->attrs[NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV6ADDR]);` and then `if (addr_len != sizeof(struct in6_addr) && addr_len != nla_len(info->attrs[NLBL_UNLABEL_A_IPV6MASK])) return -EINVAL;`. This means a short mask is accepted whenever the address length is exactly `sizeof(struct in_addr)` or `sizeof(struct in6_addr)`, because the second half of the condition is not enforced in that case. The function then returns raw pointers with `*mask = nla_data(...)`, and later code consumes them as full-sized structures: `netlbl_unlhsh_add()` dispatches by `addr_len`, and `netlbl_unlhsh_add_addr4()` reads `mask->s_addr`, while `netlbl_unlhsh_add_addr6()` reads all `mask->s6_addr32[0..3]`. Since the policy entries use `NLA_BINARY` with `.len = sizeof(struct in_addr)` / `sizeof(struct in6_addr)`, which historically enforce only a maximum length, shorter mask attributes can slip through. The fix would require exact independent validation of both address and mask lengths; that is not present here.
